title: A small share of time
hook: how small a share of endless time is given to each of us (Meditations 12.32)

segments.voice: Yesterday: you forgot, Marcus's list of things he knew and kept dropping, and each mind sharing in the divine. Your line was I forgot. Who did you see as a cousin in reason? Day six hundred thirty-five.

Open the photos on your phone and scroll back. Keep going. A year. Five. The faces get younger, the haircuts get worse, and somewhere in there is a day that seemed like it would never end. A whole life under one thumb: how much of it there is, and how fast it goes by. Marcus Aurelius had no camera roll. But near the end of his notebook, an emperor stops and measures a life, his own included, against all of time. Today: a small share.
screen: `SCROLL BACK FIVE YEARS.` → `A WHOLE LIFE UNDER YOUR THUMB.` → `A SMALL SHARE.`

segments.voice: Meditations 12.32, in George Long's translation: "How small a part of the boundless and unfathomable time is assigned to every man?" He goes on: it's swallowed up in the eternal almost at once. Then he widens the lens: how small a part of all matter, of the soul of the whole, of the earth you creep on. First, the measuring. Marcus has done this all through the book: Asia and Europe as corners of the universe, the present as a point. Here he aims it at himself. An emperor, measured against endless time, holds a tiny slice. So does everybody else. Second, why this isn't gloom. The point of 12.32 isn't that your life is worthless. It's that your share is given. Long's word is assigned: handed out, like a ration. You didn't earn it and you can't extend it. Which makes the question not how much do I have, but what do I do with the share in my hand. Third, what he does with it. Right after the measuring, the passage turns: he tells himself to think nothing great except to act as his own nature leads, and to bear what the common nature brings. Small share, plain job. Fourth, the Tuesday version. A day is a small share of a small share. You can't fill it with everything. You can fill it with a few things done as yourself, well. That's not shrinking your life. It's fitting your hands to it.
screen: `MEASURE YOUR LIFE AGAINST ALL TIME.` · `NOT WORTHLESS: ASSIGNED.` · `SMALL SHARE, PLAIN JOB.` · `A DAY IS A SHARE OF A SHARE.` · then, large: `A SMALL SHARE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Picture today as one small square on a very long ribbon of squares, before you and after you. Look only at your square. What's already in it? Work, a meal, a person, a chore. Pick one thing in today's square that matters to you, just one. Decide how you'll do it as yourself, with care. Then rest your attention on the breath, a very small share of time, and enough for now. The bell holds the time.
A small share of time. Marcus's reminder that each life is a tiny portion of endless time, given, not earned, and that the question is what we do with it. Today's word.
screen: `A SMALL SHARE OF TIME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a small share. Before bed tonight, name the one thing you spent today's share on that you'd spend it on again. Day six hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use the view of endless time as a way of sorting a day, setting the small things down and choosing a few to do well.

fork.setup: you've just pictured your life as a tiny slice of endless time. what does Marcus do next in 12.32?
options: decide nothing matters and stop trying.
tell himself to act as his nature leads and bear what comes.
plan a monument so he'll be remembered.
fork.reveal: the passage turns from measuring to a plain job: think nothing great except acting by your nature and bearing what the whole brings.

original.note: Greek: an age, eternity. The endless time Marcus measures each life against.

trapdoor: what you thought: a small share of time means life is short, so hurry.
what it means: your portion of time is given and tiny, so spend it on a few things done well, as yourself.
what a scholar hears: the cosmic perspective, the view from above, is a recurring Stoic exercise in Marcus, aimed at freeing the mind from inflated concerns, not at despair.

sources.quoted: How small a part of the boundless and unfathomable time is assigned to every man?

notes: Confirm Long 1862's exact wording of the opening of 12.32.
Confirm the end of 12.32: think nothing great except to act as one's nature leads and to bear what the common nature brings. Paraphrased.
'Asia and Europe are corners of the universe' and 'the present a point' are from 6.36. Paraphrased.
'Assigned' / 'portioned' hedged as the sense of the text (Greek ἀπομεμέρισται); confirm.
Marcus was in his fifties at the end of his life (born 121, died 180); book twelve's date is not known for certain.

Editor review (year 2): cut the unsourced age ('an emperor in his fifties') and the superlative 'the smallest share of time there is'; stopped telling the listener what they were sure of and felt; tied 'assigned' to Long's wording instead of a claim about the Greek.
